questions.stem: A security architect asks for Snowflake Tri-Secret Secure with a customer-managed key supplementing Snowflake-managed keys. If only Standard, Enterprise, and Business Critical editions are in scope, what is the minimum suitable edition?
options: Standard.
Enterprise.
Business Critical.
All three offer identical customer-managed key features.
feedback: Standard alone does not provide this feature.
Enterprise alone is below the minimum for Tri-Secret Secure.
Correct: Tri-Secret Secure is a Business Critical or higher capability.
Encryption at rest exists across editions; Tri-Secret Secure is a separate higher-edition feature.
questions.reason: Correct: Tri-Secret Secure is a Business Critical or higher capability.
questions.clue: Differentiate automatic encryption from customer-managed Tri-Secret Secure.
learn: All editions include baseline encryption.
Tri-Secret Secure requires Business Critical or higher.
Periodic data rekeying has a different edition requirement.
questions.workedExample: An Enterprise subscription can satisfy some rekeying requirements yet still not satisfy a Tri-Secret Secure mandate.
questions.examTrap: Do not merge periodic rekeying and Tri-Secret Secure into one edition rule.

questions.topic: Information Schema versus Account Usage for current objects
questions.stem: A developer needs to discover currently accessible tables in one database immediately after deployment; the audit team separately wants historical account-wide usage. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The database INFORMATION_SCHEMA is a natural place to inspect currently visible objects, subject to role privileges.
ACCOUNT_USAGE always reflects every newly created object instantly with no reporting latency.
ACCOUNT_USAGE is commonly used for account-wide historical reporting and can have view-specific latency.
INFORMATION_SCHEMA automatically exposes every object in all accounts regardless of grants.
feedback: Correct: database-scoped Information Schema metadata is permission-sensitive.
Account Usage views have documented reporting latencies.
Correct: Account Usage is useful for historical/account-wide analysis.
Information Schema is scoped and privilege filtered, not a cross-account bypass.
questions.reason: Correct: database-scoped Information Schema metadata is permission-sensitive. Correct: Account Usage is useful for historical/account-wide analysis.
questions.clue: The question contrasts fresh database-scoped discovery with historical account-wide reporting.
learn: Information Schema can provide current object metadata.
ACCOUNT_USAGE surfaces account-level history and has latency caveats.
Role visibility still governs which objects appear.
questions.workedExample: Check newly deployed tables using the database information schema; use Account Usage for trend auditing.
questions.examTrap: Do not treat the two metadata families as identical snapshots.

questions.stem: An account already encrypts all customer data. A new policy specifically requires Snowflake's PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING capability, but NOT Tri-Secret Secure. Which minimum edition among Standard, Enterprise and Business Critical supports it?
options: Standard.
Enterprise.
Business Critical, exclusively.
No Snowflake edition supports periodic rekeying.
feedback: Standard does not meet the periodic-data-rekeying edition requirement.
Correct: Enterprise or higher supports periodic rekeying.
Business Critical can support it but is not the minimum.
Snowflake documents this as a supported higher-edition feature.
questions.reason: Correct: Enterprise or higher supports periodic rekeying.
questions.clue: The requested feature is periodic rekeying, not customer-managed Tri-Secret Secure.
learn: Periodic rekeying is an Enterprise-or-higher feature.
Tri-Secret Secure instead requires Business Critical or higher.
Ordinary automatic encryption is not evidence that periodic rekeying is enabled.
questions.workedExample: For a contract mandating only periodic rekeying, Enterprise meets the edition threshold; enable the account parameter separately.
questions.examTrap: Distinguish feature availability from feature activation.

questions.stem: A VARCHAR column contains 'apac|retail|renewals'. Which expression returns only 'retail' without regex, assuming the value uses the shown delimiter?
options: SPLIT_PART(region_key, '|', 0)
SPLIT_PART(region_key, '|', 1)
SPLIT_PART(region_key, '|', 2)
SPLIT_PART(region_key, '|', 3)
feedback: Index zero is treated like position one, not the middle part.
Part one is apac.
Correct: Snowflake SPLIT_PART uses a one-based field position.
Part three is renewals.
questions.reason: Correct: Snowflake SPLIT_PART uses a one-based field position.
questions.clue: Count fields starting at one.
learn: SPLIT_PART splits a string using a literal delimiter.
Positive field positions start at 1.
Negative positions can select fields counting backward.
questions.workedExample: apac is part 1, retail is part 2, renewals is part 3.
questions.examTrap: Do not import zero-based indexing assumptions from Python.

questions.stem: A query builds a label with CONCAT_WS('-', 'active', NULL, 'premium'). The developer expects 'active-premium'. In Snowflake, what is the actual result?
options: 'active-premium' because NULL is skipped.
An empty string.
SQL NULL.
'active--premium' because NULL is replaced by an empty field.
feedback: Snowflake CONCAT_WS does not skip NULL arguments.
The result is NULL, not an empty string.
Correct: a NULL argument makes CONCAT_WS return NULL.
Snowflake does not implicitly coerce NULL to an empty string.
questions.reason: Correct: a NULL argument makes CONCAT_WS return NULL.
questions.clue: The function's NULL behavior differs across SQL dialects.
learn: CONCAT_WS returns NULL when any input argument is NULL.
COALESCE can explicitly replace NULL with a chosen string before concatenating.
Never assume a cross-database function behaves identically by name.
questions.workedExample: CONCAT_WS('-', 'active', COALESCE(NULL, ''), 'premium') can produce a double separator rather than omitting a segment.
questions.examTrap: Remember that coalescing to empty string does not automatically remove the extra delimiter.

questions.stem: A consumer has read-only imported database PARTNER_FEED and a writable local database ANALYTICS. Which TWO operations respect the sharing boundary? (Select TWO.)
options: SELECT rows from PARTNER_FEED for analysis.
CREATE TABLE ANALYTICS.PUBLIC.COPY AS SELECT ... FROM PARTNER_FEED.PUBLIC.EVENTS, if privileges allow.
UPDATE PARTNER_FEED.PUBLIC.EVENTS directly to tag consumer-owned status.
ALTER the provider's shared table to add a proprietary column.
feedback: Correct: read access is the consumer's primary capability.
Correct: materializing results into the consumer's own writable database is allowed.
Direct DML cannot modify provider-owned shared tables.
Consumers do not change provider schema definitions through a direct share.
questions.reason: Correct: read access is the consumer's primary capability. Correct: materializing results into the consumer's own writable database is allowed.
questions.clue: Reading shared data and writing local derived data are distinct rights.
learn: Provider objects in imported shares remain read-only.
Consumers can combine shared rows with local data.
The consumer controls its own local derived objects.
questions.workedExample: A local table can store joined shared order rows and private risk scores without changing the source share.
questions.examTrap: Read-only does not mean you cannot use shared rows in a local writable query.

questions.stem: A company wants an automatically refreshable copy of PROD_DB in another Snowflake account. A teammate proposes CREATE DATABASE CLONE using the source account's name. Which TWO claims are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: Ordinary zero-copy cloning is not an arbitrary cross-account database copy mechanism.
A secondary created by database replication can be refreshed from its primary.
A secondary replica becomes writable immediately after every refresh.
Secure sharing alone grants the consumer an independently writable full duplicate of provider tables.
feedback: Correct: normal CLONE syntax does not jump between accounts.
Correct: replication creates a secondary that can be refreshed.
A secondary stays read-only unless supported failover promotes it.
Shared database objects are read-only for consumers.
questions.reason: Correct: normal CLONE syntax does not jump between accounts. Correct: replication creates a secondary that can be refreshed.
questions.clue: Choose between same-account cloning, cross-account replication, and read-only sharing.
learn: Replication keeps another account's secondary database current.
A replica's writeability differs from a local zero-copy clone.
Failover is separate from basic replication refresh.
questions.workedExample: Use replication to maintain a disaster-recovery copy and failover procedures to promote it if writes are required.
questions.examTrap: Replication is not the same as Time Travel or a normal clone.

questions.stem: Database CORP has a future SELECT grant on TABLES to ROLE_REPORT. Schema CORP.FINANCE separately grants future SELECT on TABLES to ROLE_FINANCE. A new regular table is created in CORP.FINANCE. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The schema-level future grant applies to the new table.
Both database- and schema-level SELECT future grants always accumulate for the same object type.
The schema-level grant takes precedence over the database-level future grant for TABLES in that schema.
The owner of every existing table changes to ROLE_FINANCE automatically.
feedback: Correct: the schema's future privilege is materialized for its new tables.
Same-type future grants at the two levels do not simply accumulate in this situation.
Correct: the schema-level rule supersedes the corresponding database-level rule.
SELECT grants do not transfer OWNERSHIP or retroactively change old tables.
questions.reason: Correct: the schema's future privilege is materialized for its new tables. Correct: the schema-level rule supersedes the corresponding database-level rule.
questions.clue: Future-grant precedence depends on object type and scope.
learn: Future grants act on new objects, not on arbitrary old objects.
Schema-level future grants supersede database-level future grants for the same object type.
Ownership grants and regular privileges require separate consideration.
questions.workedExample: Finance-specific future grants override default database-wide future grants for newly created Finance tables.
questions.examTrap: A database future grant isn't guaranteed to grant everyone access when a schema-specific rule exists.

questions.topic: Row access policy mapping table owner rights
questions.stem: A ROW ACCESS POLICY consults a private entitlement mapping table. Analysts can SELECT the protected fact table but cannot SELECT the mapping table. Their fact-table queries work. Which TWO explanations are consistent with Snowflake? (Select TWO.)
options: Each analyst must be given direct SELECT on the mapping table or the policy cannot execute.
Policy evaluation uses the policy owner's privileges when resolving its mapping table dependencies.
The policy-owning role needs access to the mapping table used by the policy.
A table owner can bypass any row access policy just by choosing a larger warehouse.
feedback: Owner-rights policy evaluation can protect the mapping table from direct consumer access.
Correct: row access policies evaluate with the policy owner's rights.
Correct: the owner role needs suitable privileges on mapping-table dependencies.
Compute sizing does not bypass policy enforcement.
questions.reason: Correct: row access policies evaluate with the policy owner's rights. Correct: the owner role needs suitable privileges on mapping-table dependencies.
questions.clue: The hidden lookup table does not automatically require every querying role to have SELECT on it.
learn: Row access policies evaluate with owner-rights semantics.
Protected mapping tables can remain inaccessible directly to analysts.
Test owner privileges independently from analyst table privileges.
questions.workedExample: Grant the policy owner access to ENTITLEMENTS and analysts access to SALES; analysts still see only permitted SALES rows.
questions.examTrap: Don't grant sensitive entitlement mappings to all analysts just to make row policies work.

questions.stem: A publisher allows analysts to join a sensitive claims table only using CLAIM_ID; joining by EMAIL must be rejected at query compilation. Which mechanism most directly expresses such restrictions for the protected table?
options: A join policy attached to the table with CLAIM_ID as an allowed join key.
A row access policy filtering by CURRENT_ROLE alone.
An account-level resource monitor.
A default database collation setting.
feedback: Correct: join policies support join requirements and configured allowed join keys.
Row access policies restrict rows; they do not substitute for an allowed-join-key rule.
Credit controls cannot dictate legal join predicates.
Collation controls string comparison behavior, not approved join relationships.
questions.reason: Correct: join policies support join requirements and configured allowed join keys.
questions.clue: The constraint concerns JOIN operations and approved keys.
learn: Join policies can require joins against a protected table.
Allowed join keys are specified when attaching the policy to a table or view.
Policies may be applied through supported object configuration.
questions.workedExample: Attach a join policy to CLAIMS with ALLOWED JOIN KEYS (CLAIM_ID) to disallow unsupported EMAIL join patterns.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse a row-filtering policy with a policy governing joins.

questions.stem: A company uses Snowpipe and other serverless features as well as warehouses. Finance needs alerts when a group of services approaches its credit budget. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)
options: A resource monitor assigned to a virtual warehouse automatically stops every serverless service in the account.
A Snowflake budget can monitor supported objects and serverless usage and trigger notifications.
Budget alerts are not equivalent to a guaranteed account-wide automatic suspension of all compute.
Any budget requires every query to run on the same named warehouse.
feedback: Warehouse resource monitors do not comprehensively control serverless consumption.
Correct: budgets can monitor supported object/service usage and notify.
Correct: budget alerts do not guarantee shutdown of all service categories.
Budget coverage is not limited to a single chosen virtual warehouse.
questions.reason: Correct: budgets can monitor supported object/service usage and notify. Correct: budget alerts do not guarantee shutdown of all service categories.
questions.clue: The scope includes serverless spending, not only virtual warehouses.
learn: Budgets are for cost monitoring and alerts across eligible sources.
Resource monitors principally control warehouse credit usage.
Monitoring and enforced shutdown are different capabilities.
questions.workedExample: Track Snowpipe and warehouse spending in budgets, and use warehouse monitors separately when suspension is required.
questions.examTrap: Don't equate receiving a budget email with preventing every future credit charge.

questions.stem: A loader selects `$1:id::NUMBER` and `$1:total::NUMBER` from staged JSON and maps them into target columns (ORDER_ID, AMOUNT). It also sets MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME=CASE_INSENSITIVE on that COPY statement. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME cannot be combined with a COPY SELECT transformation in the same command.
Using an explicit target column list and a compatible SELECT transformation is an appropriate way to control these mappings.
CASE_INSENSITIVE makes an otherwise invalid SELECT-transformation combination legal.
Changing warehouse size resolves this SQL compilation restriction.
feedback: Correct: the two COPY mechanisms are mutually exclusive in the same statement.
Correct: explicit targets with source SELECT expressions can map fields.
The named match mode does not override the SQL restriction.
Compilation rules do not depend on warehouse horsepower.
questions.reason: Correct: the two COPY mechanisms are mutually exclusive in the same statement. Correct: explicit targets with source SELECT expressions can map fields.
questions.clue: The conflict arises from combining two valid but incompatible COPY mechanisms.
learn: COPY INTO can transform staged data through a source SELECT.
MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME is a separate mapping mechanism.
Snowflake explicitly rejects MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME with a COPY transform SELECT.
questions.workedExample: Use COPY INTO orders(order_id,amount) FROM (SELECT $1:id::NUMBER,$1:total::NUMBER FROM @stage), without MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME.
questions.examTrap: Don't try to fix SQL compatibility restrictions by changing match case.

questions.topic: CSV NULL token and empty field distinction
questions.stem: A CSV includes `NULL` for missing values and an empty unquoted field for a genuine empty VARCHAR. The target requires SQL NULL for the text token but an empty string for the empty field. Which TWO file-format settings are relevant? (Select TWO.)
options: Configure NULL_IF to recognize the literal token 'NULL'.
Set EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL=FALSE so empty CSV fields need not become SQL NULL.
Set EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL=TRUE to preserve empty strings in every case.
Set ON_ERROR=SKIP_FILE; that differentiates NULL tokens from empty strings.
feedback: Correct: NULL_IF maps specified source text tokens to SQL NULL.
Correct: EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL controls unquoted empty fields.
TRUE interprets empty fields as SQL NULL rather than preserving empty strings.
Error handling is not a substitute for file-format NULL semantics.
questions.reason: Correct: NULL_IF maps specified source text tokens to SQL NULL. Correct: EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL controls unquoted empty fields.
questions.clue: Literal NULL and empty CSV field are two different inputs.
learn: NULL_IF matches specified text tokens including 'NULL'.
EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL affects empty fields in CSV.
Inspect named file-format settings instead of assuming defaults work.
questions.workedExample: Input `A,NULL,` can represent a SQL NULL and a genuine empty VARCHAR when the two controls are set deliberately.
questions.examTrap: Always test actual CSV quoting and null-sentinel conventions.

questions.stem: An analyst wants to see all rows that a `COPY INTO @exports FROM (SELECT ...)` unload would emit, while writing no files. Which option is specifically supported for COPY INTO a location?
options: VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ERRORS.
VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS.
ON_ERROR = CONTINUE.
VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ROWS.
feedback: RETURN_ERRORS belongs to load-validation modes, not unload preview.
RETURN_ALL_ERRORS also belongs to load validation.
ON_ERROR is not the documented preview switch for an unload.
Correct: RETURN_ROWS executes the query and returns the data rather than unloading files.
questions.reason: Correct: RETURN_ROWS executes the query and returns the data rather than unloading files.
questions.clue: Unloading has a RETURN_ROWS preview option distinct from loading's error-validation options.
learn: COPY INTO <location> can use VALIDATION_MODE=RETURN_ROWS.
This mode does not unload files.
RETURN_ERRORS and RETURN_ALL_ERRORS are load-validation concepts.
questions.workedExample: Run COPY INTO @exports FROM (SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10) VALIDATION_MODE=RETURN_ROWS before removing the option to unload.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse previewing unload rows with finding errors in staged load files.

questions.stem: A timestamp-based event table spans billions of rows. A report filters `TO_VARCHAR(EVENT_TS,'YYYY-MM-DD')='2026-11-15'` and scans most micro-partitions. Which TWO observations are defensible? (Select TWO.)
options: Rewriting to `EVENT_TS >= '2026-11-15'::TIMESTAMP AND EVENT_TS < '2026-11-16'::TIMESTAMP` may improve pruning.
Applying functions to the filtered timestamp can make direct min/max range pruning less effective.
Snowflake must scan all partitions whenever a table contains a TIMESTAMP column.
Increasing multi-cluster count always restores partition pruning on the expression.
feedback: Correct: a direct half-open timestamp range often exposes useful pruning metadata.
Correct: function-wrapped predicates can obscure directly prunable ranges.
A timestamp column does not force a full scan.
Extra clusters increase concurrency capacity, not guaranteed predicate pruning.
questions.reason: Correct: a direct half-open timestamp range often exposes useful pruning metadata. Correct: function-wrapped predicates can obscure directly prunable ranges.
questions.clue: Expose raw timestamp bounds and inspect partitions scanned.
learn: Micro-partition metadata includes value ranges used in pruning.
Functions around filter columns can reduce effective pruning.
Use query profile to compare the actual partitions scanned before and after.
questions.workedExample: Compare the two predicates on the same table and inspect total vs scanned partitions in Query Profile.
questions.examTrap: More compute isn't a substitute for a prunable predicate.

questions.stem: A table records multiple sensor measurements per SENSOR_ID. The report must return one newest row per sensor using ROW_NUMBER() ordered by event time. Which TWO patterns can implement this correctly, assuming a deterministic tie-breaker is included? (Select TWO.)
options: Use `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1` directly in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
Use `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sensor_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC)=1`.
Use `HAVING ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)=1` without grouping.
Compute ROW_NUMBER() AS rn in a subquery, then filter `WHERE rn=1` outside.
feedback: Window functions are not directly filterable through WHERE at the same SELECT level.
Correct: QUALIFY filters after window functions are computed.
HAVING is not a generic replacement for QUALIFY on window results.
Correct: a subquery or CTE can expose the window result for an outer WHERE.
questions.reason: Correct: QUALIFY filters after window functions are computed. Correct: a subquery or CTE can expose the window result for an outer WHERE.
questions.clue: QUALIFY and an outer WHERE operate after the window value exists.
learn: QUALIFY is evaluated after window functions.
A CTE with rn followed by outer WHERE rn=1 is a valid alternative.
Explicit tie-breakers make latest-row selection deterministic.
questions.workedExample: SELECT ... QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY sensor_id ORDER BY ts DESC,id DESC)=1 matches a CTE producing rn then filtering rn=1.
questions.examTrap: Do not use WHERE to filter a just-computed window function in the same SELECT.

questions.stem: A secure view in PUBLISH.PUBLIC.V_EVENTS reads a protected base table in INTERNAL.PUBLIC.EVENTS. The provider wants a classic direct share exposing only the view. Which TWO steps are relevant? (Select TWO.)
options: Give the share REFERENCE_USAGE on INTERNAL so the view may reference objects in that separate database.
Grant consumers direct SELECT on the INTERNAL base table as the only supported approach.
Provide the appropriate USAGE on the published database/schema and SELECT on the secure view to the share.
Replace the secure view with an ordinary non-secure view; ordinary views are required for cross-database shares.
feedback: Correct: REFERENCE_USAGE enables the cross-database reference needed by this share.
Sharing the underlying base table directly is unnecessary for view-only exposure.
Correct: published view privileges and published database/schema visibility are still required.
Cross-database classic sharing of a view uses supported secure-view behavior.
questions.reason: Correct: REFERENCE_USAGE enables the cross-database reference needed by this share. Correct: published view privileges and published database/schema visibility are still required.
questions.clue: Reference database permission and shared view permission solve different parts.
learn: The share needs REFERENCE_USAGE for databases referenced by its shared secure view.
USAGE and SELECT grants are still needed on published objects.
Base data can remain private from the consumer as a directly shared table.
questions.workedExample: Share PUBLISH.PUBLIC.V_EVENTS while giving REFERENCE_USAGE for INTERNAL; don't expose INTERNAL.PUBLIC.EVENTS directly.
questions.examTrap: REFERENCE_USAGE does not replace USAGE/SELECT grants on the published view.

questions.topic: Local enrichment of provider shared data
questions.stem: A receiving account imports a provider's read-only sales share. Its analysts must join the shared sales records to private local fraud scores and store enriched results for downstream teams. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: The consumer can SELECT shared rows and JOIN them to local fraud tables.
The consumer can write the combined result into a local table it owns, with sufficient privileges.
The consumer can add a FRAUD_SCORE column directly to the provider-owned shared table.
A read-only share makes any consumer-side SELECT involving a local table illegal.
feedback: Correct: a consumer can join read-only shared data to local objects.
Correct: writable derived objects can be created in the consumer's database.
The provider's shared object definition cannot be modified by the consumer.
Read-only describes the shared objects, not every downstream query that references them.
questions.reason: Correct: a consumer can join read-only shared data to local objects. Correct: writable derived objects can be created in the consumer's database.
questions.clue: Data ownership stays with the provider; enrichment belongs in the consumer's database.
learn: Shares expose provider-controlled read-only objects.
Local CTAS and inserts can materialize enriched results.
Join privileges and local write privileges are checked separately.
questions.workedExample: CREATE TABLE local.enriched AS SELECT s.*, f.score FROM shared.sales s JOIN local.fraud f ON s.id=f.id.
questions.examTrap: Distinguish modifying a share from producing a local derived dataset.
